headline: Midterm count continues as Democrats gain; Canada's budget lands Thursday
briefing: Counting from Tuesday's U.S. midterms continues, with early reports pointing to Democratic gains and President Trump saying he accepts the results; final control of Congress was not confirmed in the sources checked this morning. Oil eased on hopes of an Iran-Oman deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and GTA gas is forecast to drop 11 cents today. Canada's federal budget is tabled Thursday.

keyDates.label: Israel certifies results
keyDates.why: Official results are confirmed before President Herzog consults parties on forming a government.

keyDates.label: Federal budget
keyDates.why: Finance Minister Champagne tables the budget, including the immigration levels update.

keyDates.label: U.S. October jobs report
keyDates.why: A strong report could push interest rates higher, which affects Canadian borrowing costs too.

keyDates.label: TTC Line 2 weekend closure
keyDates.why: Subway service is shut between St. George and Broadview on Nov. 7–8, and two GO lines also close that weekend.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada deliberations summary
keyDates.why: The bank publishes its Summary of Deliberations behind its rate hike, with hints on future moves.

stories.headline: Democrats gain in U.S. midterms; control of Congress still being counted
stories.summary: Counting continues after Tuesday's midterms, with early reports of Democratic gains. Trump says he accepts the results.
stories.now: Decision Desk HQ projects former governor Roy Cooper (D) wins the Senate seat in North Carolina being vacated by Republican Thom Tillis. The Guardian reports Democratic senators in Georgia (Jon Ossoff) and Virginia have won re-election, and that House Democrats are prevailing in districts redrawn to favour Republicans. Florida's Senate and governor's races remain tight. Axios reports Trump told the New York Times he is willing to accept the results, while saying Republicans lost because he was not on the ballot. Final control of the Senate and House had not been confirmed in the sources checked early Wednesday, and close races, especially where mail ballots are counted for days, may take time to call.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

timeline.event: 53M early votes; Trump's final Kansas rally
Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
Cooper projected to flip North Carolina; Ossoff holds Georgia
Trump says he accepts results; counting continues

stories.why: The result decides whether Trump's tariffs, war powers and spending face a check from Congress, or a freer hand for the next two years.
stories.impact: A Democratic Congress could push to roll back tariffs that hit Ontario steel, auto and parts plants, and to limit new Iran strikes that affect fuel prices. Final control may not be known for days.

stories.headline: Oil falls on hopes of an Iran breakthrough after limited U.S. strikes
stories.summary: Brent crude fell more than 6% to about US$105.55 on hopes of a deal, even as U.S. forces struck Iranian radar and missile sites on Qeshm Island.
stories.now: The Guardian reports Brent dropped over 6% to US$105.55 a barrel, its lowest in more than two weeks, on hopes of a breakthrough. On Monday the U.S. struck radar detectors and missile launchers on Iran's Qeshm Island, which officials described as limited and defensive, while mediators kept pushing for a deal. Al Jazeera's live coverage says Vice-President JD Vance sees progress in talks while Tehran says the ball is in Washington's court. DNC chair Ken Martin said Democrats should end the Iran war if they win power.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: U.S. and Israel begin striking Iran
Qatar hands Iran new draft deal
Trump: war ends 'one way or the other'
U.S. strikes on Qeshm Island; Brent falls to US$105.55

stories.why: Oil near or above US$100 is the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S., and it pushed the Bank of Canada to raise rates last week.
stories.impact: Lower crude should show up at GTA pumps within days, but a failed deal could send prices back up. Fuel costs feed into groceries, deliveries and transit.

sources.title: The Guardian: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Al Jazeera: Explosions hit Iran's Qeshm Island
The Hill: U.S. strikes Iranian radar, missiles

stories.headline: Canada-U.S. trade talks continue as Democrats vow to repeal tariffs
stories.summary: Tariffs on Canadian goods remain while talks continue, and the DNC chair says Democrats would move to end them if they win power.
stories.now: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday he had a good conversation with Trump and that negotiators will keep working on a deal, but no tariff relief or timeline has been announced. DNC chair Ken Martin said Democrats should repeal Trump's tariffs if they take power after the midterms, citing exit polls showing voters think the country is on the wrong track. On Oct. 30 the U.S. reshuffled its list of Canadian goods facing 50% tariffs. Trump has said steel and auto tariffs on Canada will rise to 50% on Jan. 1.
stories.backstory: Broad Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian counter-tariffs. Separate U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos hit Ontario's factories hardest. Ottawa is courting other partners while talks continue.

timeline.event: DNC chair vows tariff repeal if Democrats win power

stories.why: Ontario sells most of its steel and auto output to the U.S., so both a deal and the midterm outcome matter for factory jobs.
stories.impact: Jobs in Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and GTA parts plants stay exposed, and some imports such as paint, carpets and air conditioners may cost more.

sources.title: CP24: Carney says he had a 'good conversation' with Trump
The Hill: DNC chair says Democrats should repeal Trump tariffs

stories.headline: Federal budget Thursday to include immigration levels update
stories.summary: A government source says the annual immigration levels update will be part of Thursday's federal budget, which also targets small-business tax complexity.
stories.now: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables Budget 2026 on Thursday, Nov. 5. A government source confirmed to CityNews and Global News that the annual immigration levels update will be included. Champagne has also said the budget targets the complexity of the tax code for small businesses, which he calls a barrier to investment. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has warned deficits are deepening, and a fuel excise tax pause has been extended to Jan. 31, 2027.
stories.backstory: Champagne announced the Nov. 5 date on Oct. 20. The budget arrives while U.S. tariffs remain in place and the Bank of Canada has just raised its rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023.

timeline.event: Bank of Canada raises rate to 2.50%
Immigration levels update confirmed for budget

stories.why: The budget sets Ottawa's response to tariffs, deficits and defence spending, and the immigration targets shape population growth.
stories.impact: Watch for small-business tax changes, the deficit figure and immigration targets, which affect GTA hiring, rents and housing demand.

sources.title: Global News: Federal budget 2026 immigration

stories.headline: U of T Mississauga cancels classes after 19-year-old found dead in residence
stories.summary: A 19-year-old man was found dead in a UTM residence after an overnight police response in an intimate-partner violence incident; the SIU is investigating.
stories.now: U of T cancelled classes at its Mississauga campus Tuesday after the 19-year-old was found dead in a residence following a police response Monday night. CP24 reports he was the suspect in an intimate-partner violence incident. Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which probes deaths involving police, is investigating. Paramedics said police asked them to stage nearby and that they had treated no patients.
stories.backstory: Police responded Monday night to a report at the campus and a shelter-in-place order was issued before the standoff ended with the man found dead. The SIU is Ontario's independent civilian agency that investigates deaths and serious injuries involving police.

timeline.event: Overnight police response at UTM; shelter-in-place order
Man found dead; classes cancelled; SIU investigates

stories.why: Campus safety and police use of force are under scrutiny whenever the SIU is called.
stories.impact: Students and staff at UTM should follow the university's updates on when classes and services resume.

stories.headline: Justice Department expands probe into Alaska Senate race 'spoiler' candidate
stories.summary: The department sent target letters, including to a prominent Democratic attorney, in a criminal probe tied to a second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot.
stories.now: PBS NewsHour and Al Jazeera report the Justice Department escalated its investigation by sending target letters to a prominent Democratic lawyer in Washington and others, saying they may face charges. The probe concerns a Democratic-aligned candidate who shares a name with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Republicans accuse Democrats of recruiting a spoiler to confuse voters, while Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has denied knowing about any such plot.
stories.backstory: Sullivan and allies accused Democrats last week of recruiting a second Dan Sullivan for the ballot, and an Alaska prosecutor opened a probe. Peltola, a Democrat, is challenging Sullivan for the seat.

timeline.event: Peltola denies knowledge of alleged plot

stories.why: The case adds a federal criminal angle to a Senate race that could help decide control of the chamber.
stories.impact: There is no direct Ontario effect, but the Senate majority shapes U.S. trade and tariff policy toward Canada.

stories.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.summary: The justices quickly refused the administration's emergency request to make California set aside ballots it says may belong to noncitizens.
stories.now: The Hill and The Guardian report the Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's effort to force California officials to segregate and not count about 20,000 ballots the Justice Department says belong to likely noncitizens. The ruling is the latest judicial rebuke of administration efforts to intervene in how states run elections.
stories.backstory: The administration sued California and Los Angeles County in mid-October, arguing noncitizens were left on voter rolls. Courts are generally wary of changing voting rules close to an election, and California counts mail ballots for days after Election Day.

timeline.event: Administration sues California and LA County

stories.why: It shows courts holding the line on election procedures during the vote.
stories.impact: No direct Ontario effect, but contested counts could delay a clear result in close U.S. races.

sources.title: The Guardian: Supreme Court rules against Trump over California ballots

stories.headline: Russian bombing of Ukraine aid centre kills at least 26; Dnipro hit
stories.summary: Officials say at least 26 people died when Russian bombs hit an aid centre in Komyshuvakha, and separate strikes on Dnipro killed two and injured 20.
stories.now: Al Jazeera reports at least 26 people were killed in Russian strikes on a school used as a humanitarian aid centre in southern Ukraine, with BBC citing at least nine 3,000 kg aerial bombs. PBS earlier reported at least 31 dead with dozens missing. Zelenskyy called the attack vile. Separate Russian strikes on Dnipro killed two and injured 20, damaging homes and medical facilities. Ukraine's leader was in Berlin meeting Chancellor Merz.
stories.backstory: Russia's war on Ukraine continues in its fourth year with large air strikes on cities and villages. Peace efforts have stalled, and Canada has joined allies in sanctions and aid.

timeline.event: Kyiv loses power after massive Russian strike
G20 ministers split over Russia's attendance

stories.why: Strikes on aid sites underline how far the war is from a ceasefire.
stories.impact: Ontario's large Ukrainian-Canadian community has direct ties; federal sanctions and aid decisions come through Ottawa.

stories.headline: GTA gas prices set for 11-cent drop Wednesday, then a rise Thursday
stories.summary: Regular gasoline is forecast to fall 11 cents a litre overnight, the biggest drop in months, with a rise expected the next day.
stories.now: CityNews quotes Roger McKnight of En-Pro International forecasting an 11-cent-per-litre drop for regular gasoline in Toronto and the GTA at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday, the biggest decrease in months. The Toronto Sun reports prices are set to rise again Thursday. The drop follows crude falling on hopes of a deal to end the Iran war.
stories.backstory: Pump prices in the GTA have swung with oil during the Iran war, and in October fell about two cents a day to roughly $1.72 a litre before Brent rebounded.

timeline.event: GTA pump prices fall to lowest in two months
Brent drops over 6% on Iran hopes

stories.why: Fuel is one of the most visible costs of the Iran war for commuters.
stories.impact: Fill up Wednesday if you can; analysts expect a partial rebound Thursday.

sources.title: CityNews: Toronto, GTA gas prices 11-cent drop

stories.headline: Carney: Russia will not be allowed at world juniors hockey in Alberta
stories.summary: Prime Minister Carney said Russian players will be denied visas as other countries threaten to boycott a Russian return to international hockey.
stories.now: CityNews reports Carney says Russia will not be allowed to compete at next month's world junior hockey championship in Alberta. Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Latvia have said they will not play against Russia, and Canada was asked to follow suit. Global News describes the move as a response to the boycott threats over Russia's reinstatement.
stories.backstory: Russia was suspended from international hockey after invading Ukraine in 2022. Canada has stopped issuing visas inside Russia and denied visas to Russian junior curlers earlier this year.

timeline.event: Russian junior curlers denied Canadian visas
Carney says Russians will be denied visas

stories.why: It shows Ottawa using visa policy to enforce its stance on Russia.
stories.impact: No direct local effect, though it settles a question for fans and organizers of the tournament.

stories.headline: Toronto child hunger rates nearly double as food bank visits hit 4.1 million
stories.summary: A new report says child hunger in Toronto has nearly doubled, with food banks recording about 4.1 million visits.
stories.now: Global News reports Toronto's child hunger rates have nearly doubled and that the city saw 4.1 million food bank visits, according to a new report. A radio host called the data alarming. Families describe struggling to afford staples like milk, eggs and vegetables.
stories.backstory: Food bank use in the GTA has climbed for several years as rent, groceries and borrowing costs have risen, and this year's rate increase and weak job market add pressure.

timeline.event: Report shows child hunger nearly doubled

stories.why: Rising hunger among children is a measure of how much cost-of-living pressure is landing on families.
stories.impact: Local food banks may see more demand through winter; city and provincial funding decisions are the next thing to watch.

sources.title: Global News: Toronto's child hunger rates nearly double

stories.headline: Toronto police investigate pins and needles found in Halloween candy
stories.summary: Police are investigating two separate reports of sewing needles and pins in candy collected by children in the city's east end.
stories.now: Toronto police say two reports involve candy collected on Halloween night in two east-end neighbourhoods. In an update Tuesday, investigators issued a public safety alert and asked parents to check treats.
stories.backstory: Reports of tampered candy are rare but are taken seriously after each Halloween.
stories.why: Parents need to check treats before children eat them.
stories.impact: Check and discard any suspicious candy and report it to police.

sources.title: CityNews: Toronto police Halloween candy pins and needles

stories.headline: Greenland's parliament approves security deal with Denmark and the U.S.
stories.summary: Lawmakers voted 16-0 with seven abstentions to approve the trilateral agreement signed in September.
stories.now: PBS and Al Jazeera report Greenland's parliament approved the trilateral deal with Denmark and the U.S., following months of pressure from Trump, who has sought control of the semi-autonomous territory of a NATO ally. The vote was 16-0 with seven abstentions.
stories.backstory: Trump had pressed to control Greenland, a territory of NATO member Denmark. The three governments signed the agreement in September.
stories.why: It eases a dispute inside NATO and sets the terms of the U.S. military presence in the Arctic.
stories.impact: Canada shares the Arctic and is watching U.S. moves there closely.

sources.title: PBS NewsHour: Greenland approves trilateral deal
Al Jazeera: Greenland parliament approves security deal

stories.headline: Ontario's deficit swells to $16.9 billion as tariffs delay balanced budget
stories.summary: Ontario's fall update projects a record $16.9-billion deficit this year and $36 billion over three years.
stories.now: The Oct. 29 update puts this year's deficit 22% above the spring plan, partly because of about $3.8 billion added to a contingency fund for tariff costs. Next year's shortfall is $12.7 billion and 2028 shows a $6.7-billion deficit instead of balance. Ontario will match Ottawa's 100% write-off for business investment and adds a tax break for buyers of newly built homes.
stories.backstory: Ontario's spring budget had already run deeper deficits as U.S. tariffs hit the province's factories. The Ford government has said it will spend through the trade war.
stories.why: Bigger deficits mean more borrowing and interest costs, which can squeeze future health, school and transit spending.
stories.impact: New-home buyers may get a tax break and business owners can write off equipment faster.
